newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's protests undimmed, shootings hit Kosovo.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's protests undimmed, shootings hit Kosovo.

text.p: Serbia's marathon mass protests against President Slobodan Milosevic showed no sign of losing steam as violence in the ethnic tinderbox of Kosovo posed a new challenge to his isolated government.

Tens of thousands of opposition supporters and students mounted separate protests in Belgrade on Saturday, both in carnival mood and both demanding for a 77th day that Milosevic recognise opposition wins in November's local elections.
Fissures have been opening up within an increasingly discredited state establishment too under the relentless pressure of protests by the Zajedno (Together) coalition.

The junior party in Milosevic's leftist coalition is openly calling for opposition election triumphs to be reinstated to defuse the crisis and traditionally pro-government figures like churchmen and army officers demand the same.

Bickering between the president's Socialist Party (SPS) and his wife's Yugoslav United Left (JUL) have prevented them from forming a government in one town even after a state court ruling sidelined the opposition's claim to victory.

The independent newspaper Dnevni Telegraf said on Sunday that Zajedno convened a town council in Jagodina by itself and named executive bodies after a separate SPS-JUL council session collapsed in quarrelling over top municipal posts.

Dragan Tadic, head of Zajedno's election committee in Jagodina, was quoted by Telegraf as saying that SPS and JUL deputies would be invited to join "the legitimate Zajedno-led council session" at 10 a.m. on Monday.

Jagodina was one of 14 Serbian towns, including Belgrade, where an OSCE inquiry verified that Zajedno fairly won the vote, ruling that an SPS decision to annul the outcome because of alleged "irregularities" was fraudulent.

The killing of three ethnic Albanians by Serbian police in Kosovo province on Friday was a sharp reminder of the sectarian tensions that threaten to undo international peacemaking efforts across the Balkans.

The official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug, quoting the Serbian Interior Ministry, said three Serbian policemen were wounded when three men in a car shot at them on Friday. The police returned fire, killing all three men.
Tanjug said one of the dead was a commander of the clandestine Liberation Army of Kosovo and state television (RTS) said weapons were found in the car of the "outlaws".
RTS also showed arms, explosives and maps of state installations which it said were seized in police raids in the Albanian majority province over the past few days.

But Kosovo's main political party, the Democratic League of Kosovo, described the killings as part of a brutal Serbian crackdown involving dozens of arrests of humanitarian workers and political activists over the past week.
It appealed to the international community to persuade the Serbian authorities to halt "a campaign of terror".

Ever since Milosevic revoked Kosovo's autonomy in 1989 on grounds that ethnic Albanians were preparing to secede, Western analysts have warned that a local flare-up in violence could ignite communal hatred across the region.
Little is known about the Liberation Army of Kosovo but it has claimed attacks over the past year in which both Serbians and ethnic Albanians have been killed.

In Belgrade, the Socialists appeared increasingly divided and uncertain, with more than 1,000 schools shut by striking teachers, universities in turmoil, laywers rallying with the students and no sign of an end to the mass protests.
The demonstrators have used various ways to maintain the carnival atmosphere of their street rallies, from fancy-dress parades to protests at which people turned up with their dogs.

"Tomorrow (Sunday) night please bring a stick with you," Zajedno co-leader Vuk Draskovic told cheering supporters, "and on top of it a placard on which you will write your wishes, and we shall read them out."
